460d87d9a1f54c171321d92e1fcb47cd8c257e33.new: We also report the full sequence of experiments behind one positive result, including the unsuccessful ones. A stateful defense against adaptive evasion -- a per-scope ledger of previously rejected content -- showed no significant effect at its frozen development radius; a pre-registered re-run at a looser radius was underpowered by design, with a single control event capping its p-value at 1.0; and a re-run with seeds pre-filtered to the metric's own denominator -- a design revision made after a failure, and labelled as such -- reduced evasion from 24.6% to 0.8% (paired +0/-31, p=9.3e-10). That radius carries a 29.7% ledger-poisoning blast radius; a later sweep found that radius 0.95 keeps the effect (5/130 evasions) at 6.4%, a cost a deployment must accept explicitly. For this threat model the pooled comparison against published prompt-injection detectors should not be cited in either direction: disaggregated, this project's configurations lead by 32.1 (B13) to 37.2 (B17) points over the strongest published baseline (deberta pi v2@dev, 14.1%) on memory poisoning, while trailing an off-the-shelf classifier on one corpus that constitutes almost half the pooled denominator and is plausibly within that classifier's training data.

509d52a00b17eb5bf5f18a71dae7edaef58a31cd.new: A seventh round retired a hold-out that had been scored seven times, found that its 'development set' was the hold-out itself under a different wrapper, and built five new corpora -- three memory-poisoning, two injection -- each scored once under predictions committed in advance (45/53 held across every round-7 prediction including hold-out 8's; one more, U-2, was pre-registered but never scored). On the first memory-poisoning hold-out -- a new author family writing about a new owner -- provenance-aware admission reaches 50.3% against 20.4% for the fused content classifier and near zero for every published detector, and the lead replicates on the second (a base-model author, a third owner: 54.3% against 29.5%). On a new matched-benign injection corpus the union configurations run at 10.2%-11.0% false positives rather than the 55% previously reported, which was a property of one corpus. Neutralising untrusted memory as data halves compliance at no exclusion cost (37.4% to 18.3%), but the pre-registered claim that it composes with a cheap detector to dominate the strongest exclusion-only configuration failed: it is a trade-off along the false-positive axis.

8a7b9529a1f2785d4f7fa0af056db4576e04aa86.new: A single probe proved insufficient, which is itself a finding. The first audit used one generic task and reported a 33.7% working rate; a second pass using a task fitted to each instance's own subject disagreed in both directions -- memorygraft 13% to 86% and mpbench 30% to 74% under the fitted task, but minja 88% to 19% and dsrm 70% to 37%. Attack success is therefore a property of the attack and the task it meets, so no single-probe rate is a property of the attack alone. Membership is the union over probes, since an attacker chooses the context; both probes remain published, and their spread is the uncertainty on any per-family rate.

29f638711ccd20977db25738555d13826171a345.new: The sleeper result has an identifiable cause. The attack is designed to be a mundane, harmless-looking statement about a person's routine with no instruction in it, and its mechanism check requires exactly that; it is 100% mechanism-correct and 63% working, so the instances are valid and functional. A content-only detector that flagged such a note would also flag the benign personal notes that make up most of a memory store, so a 0% content-only rate here reflects the attack achieving its design goal rather than a defect in the detector. It is also the class that provenance and corroboration are designed to reach, which is the subject of the next section.

Ordinary-benign exclusions fell from 79/1054 (7.5%) to 0, and the framed notes remained useful (68/79 answers used them, vs 70 raw and 34 excluded). The cost is substantial: on the 109 corroboration-only attacks the agent asserted the poisoned claim 14 times framed vs 2 excluded (p=0.0018) and 40 raw -- the frame removes about two thirds of the raw effect, not all of it. It is a trade-off, offered as an option for deployments where false exclusions cost more than a minority of framed fabrications; hold-out 8 tests it once (Section 13E).

3d8acc514ee4ac0c48b1d3fda36ae935e8e234fd.new: Every result so far treats each poison as a standalone memory. Deployed memory systems consolidate: an LLM periodically summarises recent memories into a new one. This is the first measurement of the effect of consolidation on a poison, and it exercises two components Phase 14's live pilot never reached -- the propagation containment guard (no derived memories were written, so it had no ancestors) and backward-chain origin attribution. On this project's 249 own-attack instances (development data; same store, retriever, agent and harm judge as the harm study), 148 of 249 consolidated summaries repeat the poison's claim.

In realistic retrieval pools -- the top 20 memories for each of 309 harm-study tasks -- B9 places the poison on the review list in only 43 retrievals, and the lists are short (on average 0.75 items, 0.61 of them benign). When the poison is listed, risk ordering places it first in 39 of 43 cases against 33.5 expected from the default order: the surface works as designed but has little to act on. A first design that pooled unrelated items at random gave a much larger gain (precision 100% in the first 50 against 43%) but is reported only as an artifact: in a pool of unrelated items lexical divergence is positive for every item, so B9 routed 1706 of 1858 items to validation, a queue no reviewer would face.
